cultivar: Various Wuyi plants, including Shuixian and Rougui
processing: Made like other Wuyi rock teas: oxidised, twisted into strips and roasted. The name refers to where the leaf grows, not how it is made.
harvest_season: Spring, as with other Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_dry: Dark, twisted strips, as with other Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_liquor: Orange to amber, depending on the roast.
appearance_wet: Dark leaves with reddened edges, typical of Wuyi rock tea.
taste_profile: Roasted and rounded with the plant's own character, such as cinnamon in Rou Gui; generally described as having less rock character than core-area tea.

brewing.notes: Brew like other Wuyi rock teas, with boiling water and short steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and plant, as Ban Yan Rou Gui, Shui Xian or Da Hong Pao blends, usually at a far lower price than core-area tea. Boundaries between zones are not fixed in the trade, so the label depends on the seller's honesty.
description:
Ban yan, half-rock, is the middle tier of the traditional Wuyi place ladder: zheng yan, the true rock tea of the core; ban yan around its edges; and zhou cha, the lower, riverside tea. It names a zone, not a recipe.

The plants and the making are the same as elsewhere in Wuyi. What changes is the ground, and the usual view is that this tea has less of the mineral rock character.

Brew it as you would any Wuyi rock tea, with boiling water and short steeps. It is an easy, affordable way to learn the plants before paying for core-area tea.

Boundaries are loose, and the trade uses these words freely. Taste before you trust a label. A well-made ban yan tea can beat a poorly made zheng yan one.
history:
Chinese references describe ban yan tea as tea from the edges of the Wuyi area, grown on the rocks there. The zheng yan, ban yan and zhou cha ladder is widely used in writing on Wuyi tea.

Little is documented about when the term began. Its limits have never been uniformly fixed.
